title: Getting to know data

intro.text: Start from everyday examples. Read the diagrams, work through the steps, and try the questions before revealing the answers.

sections.title: Start here: what this course helps you do

blocks.text: Statistics helps us learn from data. You do not need advanced maths to begin. Start with a question, collect useful information, organize it, and explain what it tells you.

blocks.alt: A question becomes an investigation: collect, organize, summarize, then answer.
blocks.caption: A question becomes an investigation: collect, organize, summarize, then answer.

blocks.text: One story for the whole course

Imagine a university admission form. Each student gives their board, age, Class 10 marks and Class 12 marks. These answers form a dataset. We can ask how many students came from each board, what the typical marks were, and whether two sets of marks are related.

sections.title: What is statistics? Population and sample

blocks.text: Statistics is the process of collecting, describing and analyzing data so we can learn something. Data are the recorded facts and figures: numbers, labels, answers, or measurements.

blocks.alt: Population, sample, description and inference in one college travel survey.
blocks.caption: Population, sample, description and inference in one college travel survey.

blocks.text: Population means the whole group you care about

The population depends on your question. For house prices in Tamil Nadu, the population is all houses included in that question. For visitors to a city mall in a particular month, it is the people who visited that mall during that month. Define the place and time carefully.
A sample is a subgroup of the population studied in detail. If asking all 1,000 students is difficult, we might ask 100. Studying the whole population is a census.
Descriptive statistics: describe what you observed

Suppose 60 of the 100 students surveyed use the bus. Saying “60% of the students in our survey use the bus” describes the observed sample. Tables, charts and numerical summaries are descriptive tools. You can describe either a sample or an entire population.
Inferential statistics: go beyond what you observed

Using those 100 students to estimate the bus-use share among all 1,000 is inference. The sample may not match the population perfectly. Chance creates uncertainty; probability helps us reason about it. A convenient sample can also be biased: asking only students standing at the bus stop is unlikely to represent everyone.

rows: The 100 surveyed students include 60 bus users.
About 60% of all college students may use the bus.
It extends from the sample to the population.
Every house in the city was counted and summarized.
Summarizing a population is still description.

blocks.text: The purpose of a statement decides whether it is descriptive or inferential. Merely using a sample does not automatically make a study inferential.

blocks.question: We record car sales at 20 dealerships and report only their total. Is that inference?
blocks.answer: No. Reporting those observed dealerships is descriptive. Estimating sales across all dealerships would be inferential.

sections.title: Data tables: cases, variables and context

blocks.text: A dataset is a collection of related observations. Before calculating anything, find out what one row means and what each column records.

blocks.alt: Rows are students, columns are characteristics, and a cell contains one recorded value.
blocks.caption: Rows are students, columns are characteristics, and a cell contains one recorded value.

blocks.text: Cases are the units we study
A case, also called an observation, is a unit from which we collect data. It might be a student, house, car sale, day, or event. In the illustrated table, each of the three students is one case.
Variables are the characteristics we record

A variable is a characteristic that can vary across cases. In the table, student name, board, marks and height are four recorded variables. A value is one entry: 162 cm is Asha’s height. Names and IDs help identify cases; they are usually not useful quantities to average.
Why context matters

The number 84 alone is unclear. Is it marks, age, price, or temperature? A useful dataset records who or what was measured, the variable names, units, time and source. Use the same unit within a numerical column.
Where data come from

Sometimes data already exist in published reports or downloadable files. Otherwise we need to collect or generate them, for example with a survey, an experiment, or a measuring instrument. The lectures mainly assume data are available and focus on analyzing them.

An unstructured pile of notes, messages or comments is harder to analyze than a consistent table. Organizing data gives it a structure: one case per row, one variable per column, and one value per cell.
Comments can reveal opinions, but commenters are not automatically a representative sample of everyone who watched a video or used a product.

sections.title: Types of data: labels, amounts and time

blocks.text: Data can be classified in more than one way. First ask whether a value is a label or an amount. Separately ask whether the observations are a snapshot or a sequence over time.

blocks.alt: Categorical versus numerical describes the values; cross-sectional versus time series describes timing.
blocks.caption: Categorical versus numerical describes the values; cross-sectional versus time series describes timing.

blocks.text: Categorical data: which group?

Categorical, or qualitative, data identify a group or category. Examples are board, blood group, and product type. A number can still be a category code: a roll number or a code for a board does not measure an amount.
Numerical data: how much or how many?

Numerical, or quantitative, data describe amounts. Examples are weight in kilograms, height in centimeters, price in rupees, and the number of siblings. Counts are often discrete; measured quantities can be continuous. This distinction will matter more later.
Numerical measurements need units. Convert before comparing: 1.6 meters and 160 centimeters are the same height. Storing both as 1.6 and 160 in a column labeled “cm” would create a false difference.

blocks.alt: Snapshot: three cities on the same day. Time series: one city measured Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in chronological order.
blocks.caption: Same temperatures, different context: compare cities in a snapshot, or follow one city through time.

blocks.text: Cross-sectional data: a snapshot
Cross-sectional data are observed for different cases at roughly the same time. Heights of 30 students measured today or house prices across a city for one period are examples.
Time-series data: follow time

A time series records a quantity over time, such as Chennai’s daily temperature during a month. A timeplot places time in chronological order along the horizontal axis and the recorded value on the vertical axis. Sorting the dates by temperature would hide the time pattern.

rows: Blood groups of a class today
Chennai temperature each day in June

sections.title: Scales of measurement: nominal to ratio

blocks.text: A measurement scale tells us which comparisons make sense. A label, an ordered label and a measured amount give us different kinds of information.

blocks.alt: Four measurement scales with the comparison each one supports.
blocks.caption: Four measurement scales with the comparison each one supports.

blocks.text: Nominal: names with no built-in order

Nominal values identify categories without ranking them. Names, boards and blood groups are examples. Coding blood group A as 1 and B as 2 is allowed, but code 2 does not mean twice as much blood group. Changing the codes does not change the category information.
Ordinal: labels with an order

Ordinal categories have a meaningful ranking. Poor, Good and Excellent can be arranged from lower to higher service quality. T-shirt sizes Small, Medium and Large also have order. The distance from Poor to Good need not equal the distance from Good to Excellent. Do not assume equal gaps from codes 1, 2 and 3.
Interval: equal gaps, but an arbitrary zero

Interval data are numerical, and differences have a fixed meaning. In Celsius, the difference between 20°C and 40°C is 20°C. But 0°C does not mean no thermal energy. So 40°C is not twice as hot as 20°C in a meaningful ratio sense.

The same room at 20°C is 68°F; outdoors at 40°C is 104°F. The ratio changes from 40/20 = 2 to 104/68 ≈ 1.53 when the temperature scale changes. That is why Celsius ratios do not measure “twice as hot”.
Ratio: equal gaps and a meaningful zero

Ratio data have a zero that represents absence of the measured quantity, so ratios make sense. A 4 kg mass is twice a 2 kg mass. Height, elapsed time, age measured as elapsed time, and counts are standard examples. Kelvin temperature has a meaningful absolute zero.
The lecture lists marks as ratio data: 80 marks is twice 40 marks as a score. This does not mean twice the knowledge or ability. A comparison is meaningful only for the quantity actually measured.
The way you ask changes the data

The broad topic “temperature” does not have one scale for every question. “Comfortable or uncomfortable?” records nominal comfort labels. “Cold, warm or hot?” records ordered categories. A Celsius reading is interval. A Kelvin reading is ratio.

blocks.question: A runner finishes first, second or third. Does third take three times as long as first?
blocks.answer: No. Rank is ordinal. Actual finishing time is a different variable and is ratio-scaled.

sections.title: Try it: build and explore a small dataset
sections.source: Week 1 learning objectives in Course Overview.pdf and Lectures 1.1–1.4.pdf

blocks.text: This guided activity turns the Week 1 learning objectives into a practical routine. The dataset below is a small teaching example, not actual university admissions data.

blocks.alt: A practical workflow for a first student dataset.
blocks.caption: A practical workflow for a first student dataset.

blocks.text: Practice dataset
1. Create or download a table

Enter the header once, then one student per row. If using an existing CSV file, open or import it into a spreadsheet and check that columns have separated correctly. Record the source, date, population covered, and units. Keep a copy before editing.
2. Check before calculating

Look for missing entries, accidental duplicate rows and inconsistent spellings. “CBSE”, “cbse” and “CBSE ” should not become three boards. Check whether 84 means marks out of 100 or a percentage. Do not silently treat a missing mark as zero.
3. Sort, filter and choose columns

Sorting by marks rearranges the rows. Always sort the whole table together so each student keeps their own board and height. Filtering Board = CBSE keeps S01 and S03: 2 cases. Selecting Board and Marks keeps 2 columns; it does not change how many rows are selected.
4. Ask questions the data can answer

rows: How many of these five students came from CBSE?
Which listed student has the highest marks?
What percentage of all Indian students use CBSE?
No: these five do not establish a national percentage.
Does a particular board cause higher marks?
No: this small observational table cannot establish causation.
How do marks change month by month?
No: there is no repeated monthly measurement.

blocks.text: 5. Explain the result with its scope
Say “2 of these 5 students are from CBSE”, rather than leaving the group unstated. A good answer includes the group studied, the variable, the unit or denominator, and any important limitation.

blocks.answer: S03 (91) and S04 (88). Two cases remain, with all four recorded columns if no columns were removed.

blocks.answer: Zero means an actual score of zero; missing means the score is unknown. Replacing unknown marks with zero can lower the average and change conclusions. Keep missing values clearly identified.

blocks.question: 23. A table contains age and marks but no attendance information. Can it answer whether attendance is related to marks?
blocks.answer: No. Attendance was not recorded. You need the required variables paired for the same students before exploring their relationship.

blocks.question: 24. We ask 15 friends and estimate the preferences of every teenager in India. What makes that conclusion weak?
blocks.answer: The sample is small and selected from friends, who may share similar backgrounds or preferences. It is not automatically representative of all Indian teenagers.
